entities.name: Ark of the Covenant
entities.label: Evidence
entities.summary:
The Ark of the Covenant was the most sacred religious artifact of the ancient Israelites — a gold-plated acacia wood chest built at God’s instruction to Moses on Mount Sinai. It housed the Tablets of the Law (Ten Commandments), a golden jar of manna, and Aaron’s rod that budded. Carried by Levite priests 2,000 cubits ahead of the people during the wilderness wanderings, it served as the focal point of divine presence: God spoke to Moses from between the two cherubim on its mercy seat.

The Ark was central to the crossing of the Jordan, the fall of Jericho, and the establishment of worship at Shiloh, before being captured by the Philistines and later recovered. King David brought it to Jerusalem with great celebration, and Solomon enshrined it in the Holy of Holies of the First Temple. Its fate after the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BCE remains one of history’s greatest mysteries, with traditions placing it in Babylon, a cave on Mount Nebo, underground chambers beneath the Temple Mount, or the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion in Axum, Ethiopia.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Ark of the Covenant played a pivotal role in shaping the ancient Israelites' relationship with God, influencing their worship practices and informing key events such as the crossing of the Jordan and the fall of Jericho. Its presence also had significant regional implications, contributing to the establishment of Jerusalem as a major center of worship.
